subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Railway Ticket Mystery
hook: Raj discovers that numbers hide deep secrets at a railway station.

slides.title: At the Railway Station
slides.storyContext: Raj is queuing for tickets at Delhi Railway Station. The station master Mr. Sharma is distributing 240 and 180 tickets equally among different counters. Raj wonders: what is the largest number of counters that can receive equal tickets?

slides.title: Euclid's Division Lemma

points.label: Definition
points.text: For any two positive integers a and b, there exist unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing a larger number by a smaller one always leaves a remainder smaller than the divisor.

points.label: HCF(240, 180) = 60
points.text: The station can use 60 counters, each getting 4 + 3 = 7 tickets total.

example.problem: Find HCF(455, 130)

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

points.label: Theorem
points.text: Every integer greater than 1 is either prime or can be uniquely expressed as a product of primes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any number can be broken into prime building blocks in only one way.

points.label: Formula
points.text: For any two numbers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example.problem: If HCF(12, 18) = 6, find LCM(12, 18)

slides.title: Proving √2 is Irrational

points.label: Assume
points.text: √2 = p/q where p, q are coprime integers (HCF = 1)

points.label: Square
points.text: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q²

points.label: Conclusion
points.text: This means p² is even, so p is even. Let p = 2m. Then 4m² = 2q², so q² = 2m², making q even too.

points.label: Contradiction
points.text: Both p and q are even, contradicting our assumption they were coprime. Therefore √2 is irrational.

slides.inSimpleWords: √2 cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.

points.label: Terminating
points.text: 1/8 = 0.125 (ends after 3 decimal places)

points.label: Non-Terminating Repeating
points.text: 1/3 = 0.333... (repeats forever)

points.label: Rule
points.text: p/q is terminating if q = 2^a × 5^b (only factors 2 and 5)

example.problem: Is 7/80 terminating or repeating?
The station master needs to pack 48 mathematics books and 36 science books into identical kits with no books left over. What is the maximum number of kits?
example.solution: Find HCF(48, 36). 48 = 36 × 1 + 12; 36 = 12 × 3 + 0. HCF = 12 kits. Each kit has 48/12 = 4 math books and 36/12 = 3 science books.

example.problem: Two buses leave a station together at 8 AM. Bus A returns every 120 minutes and Bus B every 180 minutes. When will both buses be at the station together again?
example.solution: Find LCM(120, 180). 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Answer: 2 PM.

points.text: Euclid's Division Lemma: a = bq + r (0 ≤ r < b)
Fundamental Theorem: every number is a unique product of primes
HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
√2 is irrational (cannot be written as p/q)
p/q terminates only if denominator has only factors 2 and 5

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Garden Design
hook: A student uses polynomials to design the perfect garden layout.

slides.title: Designing a Rectangular Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandmother has 50 meters of fencing. Priya wants to design a rectangular garden where the area is maximized. She writes: Area = x(25 - x). Arjun says this is a polynomial!

slides.title: Polynomial Definition and Degree

points.label: Definition
points.text: A polynomial in x is p(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + ... + aₙxⁿ where coefficients are real numbers and n is a non-negative integer.

points.label: Degree
points.text: The highest power of x. Example: p(x) = 2x³ + 5x - 3 has degree 3.

points.label: Types
points.text: Linear (degree 1), Quadratic (degree 2), Cubic (degree 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: A polynomial is an expression with x raised to various powers, combined with numbers.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A value r is a zero of p(x) if p(r) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: For p(x) = x² - 5x + 6, if x = 2: p(2) = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. So 2 is a zero.

example.problem: Find a zero of p(x) = x² - 9
example.solution: p(3) = 9 - 9 = 0. So x = 3 is a zero. Also x = -3.

slides.title: Remainder Theorem

points.label: Theorem
points.text: If polynomial p(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is p(a).

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide p(x) = x³ - 2x² + 5 by (x - 1). Remainder = p(1) = 1 - 2 + 5 = 4

slides.inSimpleWords: When dividing a polynomial by (x - a), just plug in a to get the remainder.

points.label: Theorem
points.text: (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Is (x - 2) a factor of p(x) = x³ - 4x² + 5x - 2? Check: p(2) = 8 - 16 + 10 - 2 = 0. Yes!

example.problem: Show (x + 1) is a factor of p(x) = x³ + 2x² - x - 2

slides.title: Factorization of Quadratic Polynomials

points.label: Method
points.text: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b.

points.label: Example
points.text: x² + 7x + 12: two numbers are 3 and 4 (3×4=12, 3+4=7). So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Break a quadratic into two simple factors.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide 2x² + 5x + 2 by x + 2. Quotient = 2x + 1, Remainder = 0. So 2x² + 5x + 2 = (x + 2)(2x + 1)

example.problem: Factorize 2x³ - x² - 5x + 2 completely
Priya's garden area is A(x) = x(25 - x) = 25x - x². What are the zeros? When is area maximized?
example.solution: Zeros: 25x - x² = 0 → x(25 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 25. Maximum at vertex x = 12.5 meters, giving A = 156.25 m².

points.text: Polynomial: sum of terms with variables raised to whole number powers
Zero: a value where p(x) = 0
Remainder Theorem: remainder when dividing by (x - a) is p(a)
Factor Theorem: (x - a) is a factor iff p(a) = 0
Quadratic factorization: find two numbers with product ac and sum b

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Rohit and Neha's Coffee Shop Plan
hook: Two friends plan to open a cafe and need math to figure out prices and quantities.

slides.title: Pair of Linear Equations: Graphical and Algebraic Solutions
Opening a Coffee Shop
slides.storyContext: Rohit and Neha want to open a small cafe in Bangalore. They can spend ₹50,000 on equipment and supplies. Coffee makers cost ₹5,000 each and grinders cost ₹3,000 each. They want 6 items total. How many of each should they buy?

slides.title: Linear Equation in Two Variables

points.label: Definition
points.text: An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a, b ≠ 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Number of items: x + y = 6 (where x = coffee makers, y = grinders)

points.label: Solution
points.text: Any pair (x, y) satisfying the equation. For x + y = 6: (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), etc.

slides.inSimpleWords: An equation with two variables forms a straight line when graphed.

slides.title: System of Linear Equations

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two equations: 5000x + 3000y = 50000 (money) and x + y = 6 (count)

points.label: Solution
points.text: The pair (x, y) that satisfies BOTH equations simultaneously.

points.label: Simplified
points.text: Divide first by 1000: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: Find values of x and y that work in both equations at the same time.

slides.title: Substitution Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: From x + y = 6, express y = 6 - x

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Substitute in 5x + 3y = 50: 5x + 3(6 - x) = 50

points.label: Wait
points.text: x = 16 but x + y = 6? This means they can't buy only 6 items for ₹50,000 at these prices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Given: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Multiply second by 3: 3x + 3y = 18

example.problem: Solve: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2
example.solution: Add: 3x = 9 → x = 3. Substitute: 3 - y = 2 → y = 1. Solution: (3, 1)

points.label: Unique Solution
points.text: Lines intersect at one point (a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂). Example: 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1

points.label: No Solution
points.text: Lines are parallel (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂). Example: x + y = 5 and x + y = 10

points.label: Infinite Solutions
points.text: Lines are identical (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂). Example: 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 3

slides.title: Graphical Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Plot both lines on a coordinate grid.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Find the point where lines intersect.

points.label: Example
points.text: For x + y = 6: passes through (0, 6) and (6, 0). For 5x + 3y = 50: passes through (0, 16.67) and (10, 0)

slides.inSimpleWords: Graph both equations and see where the lines cross.

example.problem: Revised: Rohit and Neha want to buy espresso machines (₹8,000 each) and milk frothers (₹2,000 each) totaling ₹32,000 and 5 items. How many of each?
example.solution: Equations: 8x + 2y = 32 (divide by 2: 4x + y = 16) and x + y = 5. From second: y = 5 - x. Substitute: 4x + (5 - x) = 16 → 3x = 11 → x = 11/3 ≈ 3.67. Not a whole number. Try: 8x + 2y = 30 and x + y = 5. Then y = 5 - x → 8x + 2(5 - x) = 30 → 6x = 20 → x = 10/3. Still fractional. Real solution with whole numbers: x = 3 espresso, y = 2 frothers costs ₹28,000 (within budget).

example.problem: At a vegetable market, Priya buys 2 kg of tomatoes and 3 kg of onions for ₹170. Neha buys 1 kg of tomatoes and 2 kg of onions for ₹100. Find the price per kg of each.
example.solution: Let x = price of tomato/kg, y = price of onion/kg. Equations: 2x + 3y = 170 and x + 2y = 100. From second: x = 100 - 2y. Substitute: 2(100 - 2y) + 3y = 170 → 200 - 4y + 3y = 170 → y = 30. Then x = 100 - 60 = 40. Tomatoes ₹40/kg, onions ₹30/kg.

points.text: Linear equation in 2 variables: ax + by + c = 0 (straight line)
Substitution method: solve one for a variable, substitute in other
Elimination method: multiply to make coefficients equal, then subtract
Three types: unique solution (lines intersect), no solution (parallel), infinite (same line)
Graphical method: plot both lines and find intersection point

subject: Mathematics
title: Aman's Swimming Pool Project
hook: A student uses quadratic equations to design a perfect swimming pool.

slides.title: Building a Home Swimming Pool
slides.storyContext: Aman's family wants to build a rectangular swimming pool with a 4-meter concrete border around it. The outer dimensions are 20m × 16m. Aman needs to find the inner pool dimensions such that the border area equals the pool area. He discovers this leads to a quadratic equation!

slides.title: Quadratic Equation Definition

points.label: Standard Form
points.text: ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0 (if a = 0, it's linear, not quadratic)

points.label: Degree
points.text: Always degree 2 (highest power of x is 2)

slides.inSimpleWords: A quadratic equation has x² as the highest power term.

points.label: Method
points.text: Express ax² + bx + c as (px + q)(rx + s) = 0

example.problem: Solve 2x² - 8x + 6 = 0

slides.title: Completing the Square

points.label: Process
points.text: Convert ax² + bx + c = 0 to (x + p)² = q form

slides.inSimpleWords: Rearrange the equation so one side becomes a perfect square.

example.problem: Solve x² + 4x - 5 = 0

points.label: Discriminant
points.text: Δ = b² - 4ac

points.label: If Δ > 0
points.text: Two distinct real roots

points.label: If Δ = 0
points.text: One repeated real root (x = -b/2a)

points.label: If Δ < 0
points.text: No real roots (complex roots)

example.problem: Check nature of roots for x² - 4x + 4 = 0

slides.title: Applications: Sum and Product of Roots

points.label: Sum of roots
points.text: α + β = -b/a

points.label: Product of roots
points.text: αβ = c/a

points.label: Use
points.text: If roots are 3 and 4, then equation is x² - 7x + 12 = 0 (since sum = 7, product = 12)

example.problem: Inner pool dimensions: Let inner length = x, inner width = y. Border area = Pool area. Outer 20×16, border width = 4 on all sides. Setup: (20-8)(16-8) = (xy)/2... Simplified: find x if pool area = (20-2x)(16-2x) and border area = 320 - (20-2x)(16-2x). Let's use x² - 18x + 77 = 0.
example.solution: x = [18 ± √(324 - 308)] / 2 = [18 ± 4] / 2 → x = 11 or x = 7. Both valid dimensions: pool could be 11×7 meters or similar proportions.

example.problem: A ball is thrown upward with initial velocity 20 m/s. Its height at time t is h(t) = -5t² + 20t. When does it return to ground level (h = 0)?
example.solution: -5t² + 20t = 0 → t(-5t + 20) = 0 → t = 0 or t = 4. Ball returns at 4 seconds.

points.text: Quadratic: ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0)
Solutions by factorization: find factors (px + q)(rx + s) = 0
Quadratic formula: x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / 2a
Discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac determines nature of roots
Sum of roots = -b/a, Product of roots = c/a

subject: Mathematics
title: Sanjay's Salary Growth
hook: A young professional tracks his salary increases using arithmetic progressions.

slides.title: Annual Salary Raises
slides.storyContext: Sanjay starts his job at a tech company in Bangalore with a salary of ₹3,00,000. His manager promises a fixed raise of ₹25,000 every year. Sanjay wonders: what will be his salary in year 10? How much will he earn in total over 10 years?

slides.title: Arithmetic Progression (AP) Definition

points.label: Definition
points.text: A sequence where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.

points.label: Example
points.text: 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, ... (common difference d = 5)

slides.inSimpleWords: A list of numbers with constant gaps between them.

points.label: Formula
points.text: aₙ = a + (n-1)d, where a = first term, d = common difference

example.problem: Find the 15th term of AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, ...

slides.title: Sum of n Terms

points.label: Formula 2
points.text: Sₙ = n/2 × (first term + last term)

slides.inSimpleWords: Add up all terms in an arithmetic sequence using a quick formula.

example.problem: Why does Sₙ = n/2 × (first + last)?
example.solution: Sum = a + (a+d) + (a+2d) + ... + (a+(n-1)d). Reverse: Sum = (a+(n-1)d) + ... + (a+d) + a. Add both: 2×Sum = [2a+(n-1)d] + [2a+(n-1)d] + ... (n times) = n×[2a+(n-1)d]. So Sₙ = n/2 × [2a+(n-1)d] = n/2 × (first + last).

slides.title: Finding Common Difference and Missing Terms

points.label: Common difference
points.text: d = aₙ₊₁ - aₙ = (second term) - (first term)

points.label: Missing terms
points.text: If AP is 3, ___, 13, then middle term = (3 + 13)/2 = 8

example.problem: Insert 3 numbers between 2 and 14 to form an AP
example.solution: We need AP: 2, a₂, a₃, a₄, 14 (5 terms total). d = (14-2)/(5-1) = 3. AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14

points.label: Property 1
points.text: If a, b, c are in AP, then 2b = a + c (middle term is average)

points.label: Property 2
points.text: Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁ = aₙ (the nth term equals sum of n terms minus sum of (n-1) terms)

points.label: Property 3
points.text: Terms equidistant from start and end have equal sum

example.problem: A school library buys books in an AP pattern. Year 1: 50 books, Year 2: 100 books, Year 3: 150 books, etc. How many books in Year 20? Total books by end of Year 20?
A stadium arranges seats in rows. Row 1 has 20 seats, Row 2 has 25 seats, Row 3 has 30 seats, and so on. There are 15 rows total. What is the total seating capacity?

points.text: AP: sequence with constant difference d between consecutive terms
nth term: aₙ = a + (n-1)d
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = n/2 × (2a + (n-1)d) or n/2 × (first + last)
For 3 terms in AP: 2b = a + c
Real use: salary growth, library books, stadium seating

subject: Mathematics
title: Ananya's Bridge Design
hook: A civil engineer uses triangle similarity to design a bridge across a river.

slides.title: Measuring Across the River
slides.storyContext: Ananya needs to find the width of a river without crossing it. She places stakes on one bank and measures distances to a tree on the opposite bank. Using similar triangles, she can calculate the river width without actually measuring it!

slides.title: Triangle Congruence Criteria

points.label: SSS
points.text: Side-Side-Side: All three sides equal

points.label: SAS
points.text: Side-Angle-Side: Two sides and included angle equal

points.label: ASA
points.text: Angle-Side-Angle: Two angles and included side equal

points.label: RHS
points.text: Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side: For right triangles

slides.inSimpleWords: Two triangles are congruent if they have the same shape and size.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Triangles are similar (~) if corresponding angles are equal and sides are proportional.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle PQR means: ∠A=∠P, ∠B=∠Q, ∠C=∠R and AB/PQ = BC/QR = AC/PR

points.label: Scale factor
points.text: If AB/PQ = 2, then PQR is half the size of ABC

slides.title: AA (Angle-Angle) Similarity

points.label: Criterion
points.text: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, triangles are similar.

points.label: Why
points.text: Since angles in a triangle sum to 180°, if 2 angles match, the 3rd must also match.

points.label: Example
points.text: Triangle ABC with ∠A=60°, ∠B=70° and Triangle PQR with ∠P=60°, ∠Q=70° are similar.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two angles match, the triangles must be similar.

points.label: Theorem
points.text: If a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the other two sides, it divides them proportionally.

points.label: Statement
points.text: If DE ∥ BC in triangle ABC, then AD/DB = AE/EC

points.label: Use
points.text: Finding unknown segment lengths

example.problem: In triangle ABC, DE ∥ BC. If AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5, find EC

slides.title: Similar Triangles in Real Life: River Crossing

points.label: Setup
points.text: Ananya places a stake at point A on one bank and measures AB = 10m along the bank to point B.

points.label: Measurement
points.text: At A, she faces the tree T on the opposite bank. She walks perpendicular 6m to point C, then finds the point D where C, T, and another stake align.

points.label: Calculation
points.text: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle D'TC' (by AA similarity). If CD = 4m, river width AT = (AB × CD) / AC

slides.inSimpleWords: Use similar triangle ratios to find unknown distances.

points.label: Theorem
points.text: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² (where c is hypotenuse)

points.label: Converse
points.text: If a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled.

example.problem: A ladder 13m long leans against a wall. Base is 5m from wall. How high does it reach?

Ananya stands at point A. She marks a line AB = 100m along the bank. At A, she sights a tree T across the river. From point B, the angle ABT = 30° and angle TAB = 90° (she stands perpendicular to river). Using similar triangles, find AT (river width).
example.solution: In triangle ABT: angle TAB = 90°, AB = 100m. In similar triangle formed by her measurements, if she measures a proportional distance: tan(30°) = AT/AB → AT = 100 × tan(30°) = 100/√3 ≈ 57.7m

example.problem: A vertical pole casts a shadow of 12m when the sun is at 45° elevation. A nearby tree casts a shadow of 18m at the same time. Find the tree's height.
example.solution: Pole height/shadow = tan(45°) = 1 → Pole height = 12m. Tree and pole triangles are similar: Tree height / 18 = 12/12 = 1 → Tree height = 18m.

points.text: Congruent triangles: same shape AND size (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)
Similar triangles: same shape, different size (AA criterion)
BPT: parallel line divides sides proportionally
Pythagoras: a² + b² = c² in right triangles
Applications: surveying, shadows, bridge design

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's GPS Navigation
hook: A delivery driver uses coordinates to map out his route across the city.

slides.title: Coordinate Geometry: Points, Lines, and Distances
Delivering Across Delhi
slides.storyContext: Raj is a delivery driver for an e-commerce company in Delhi. His manager gives him coordinates of three delivery locations: Office (0,0), Customer A (3,4), Customer B (6,0). Raj needs to find the shortest route and the distances between locations.

slides.title: Cartesian Coordinate System

points.label: Axes
points.text: x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) intersect at origin (0,0)

points.label: Point notation
points.text: P(x, y) where x is horizontal distance, y is vertical distance from origin

slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate system to locate any point on a 2D plane using two numbers.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is √[(x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²]

points.label: Example
points.text: Distance from Office (0,0) to Customer A (3,4): √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 km

example.problem: Find distance between (1,2) and (4,6)

slides.title: Section Formula: Dividing a Line Segment

points.label: Internal Division
points.text: If P divides segment AB in ratio m:n internally, then P = [(mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n)]

points.label: Midpoint (1:1)
points.text: Midpoint M = [(x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2]

points.label: Example
points.text: Midpoint of Office (0,0) and Customer A (3,4): M = (1.5, 2)

slides.inSimpleWords: Find a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Slope m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁) = rise/run

points.label: Example
points.text: Slope from Office (0,0) to Customer A (3,4): m = 4/3 (steep upward)

points.label: Special cases
points.text: Horizontal line: m = 0; Vertical line: m = undefined; Perpendicular lines: m₁ × m₂ = -1

points.label: General form
points.text: ax + by + c = 0

points.label: Slope-intercept
points.text: y = mx + b (where b is y-intercept)

points.label: Point-slope
points.text: y - y₁ = m(x - x₁)

points.label: Example
points.text: Line through (0,0) with slope 4/3: y = (4/3)x or 4x - 3y = 0

example.problem: Find equation of line through (2,3) with slope 2

slides.title: Area of a Triangle using Coordinates

points.label: Formula
points.text: For triangle with vertices A(x₁,y₁), B(x₂,y₂), C(x₃,y₃): Area = |x₁(y₂-y₃) + x₂(y₃-y₁) + x₃(y₁-y₂)|/2

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate the area enclosed by three points.

example.problem: Raj has 3 stops: Office O(0,0), Customer A(3,4), Customer B(6,0). Find: (1) distance OA, (2) distance AB, (3) is O-A-B a right triangle?
example.solution: OA = √(9+16) = 5km. AB = √[(6-3)²+(0-4)²] = √[9+16] = 5km. OB = 6km. Check: 5² + 5² = 50 ≠ 36. Not right triangle. Angles: tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53.1°

example.problem: Four cities at A(0,0), B(4,0), C(4,3), D(0,3) form a rectangle. Find the diagonals' lengths and their intersection point.
example.solution: Diagonal AC = √(16+9) = 5. Diagonal BD = √(16+9) = 5. Intersection (midpoint of both) = (2, 1.5).

points.text: Distance formula: d = √[(x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²]
Section formula: point dividing segment in ratio m:n
Midpoint: [(x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2]
Slope: m = (y₂-y₁)/(x₂-x₁)
Area of triangle: use determinant formula with coordinates

subject: Mathematics
title: Kavya's Sky-High Climb
hook: A mountain climber uses trigonometry to measure heights and angles of ascent.

slides.title: Measuring Mountain Heights
slides.storyContext: Kavya is climbing in the Himalayas. Her guide tells her the elevation angle to the mountain peak is 30°. From her current position, she can see the peak at this angle. Her guide says they are 1000 meters horizontally from the peak's base. Kavya realizes she can use trigonometry to find the peak's height!

slides.title: Right Triangle Trigonometric Ratios

points.label: Sine
points.text: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse

points.label: Cosine
points.text: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse

points.label: Tangent
points.text: tan θ = opposite/adjacent

points.label: Reciprocals
points.text: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ

slides.inSimpleWords: Ratios of sides in a right triangle compared to angles.

slides.title: Standard Angle Values

points.text: sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° = undefined

slides.inSimpleWords: Standard angle values are fixed and worth memorizing.

points.label: Pythagorean
points.text: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1

points.label: Tangent-Secant
points.text: 1 + tan² θ = sec² θ

points.label: Cotangent-Cosecant
points.text: 1 + cot² θ = cosec² θ

points.label: Use
points.text: Simplify trigonometric expressions

example.problem: If sin θ = 3/5, find cos θ (in first quadrant)
example.solution: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 → (3/5)² + cos² θ = 1 → 9/25 + cos² θ = 1 → cos² θ = 16/25 → cos θ = 4/5

slides.title: Complementary Angle Relations

points.label: Theorem
points.text: sin θ = cos(90° - θ) and cos θ = sin(90° - θ)

slides.inSimpleWords: Sine and cosine of complementary angles are equal.

points.label: Quadrant I
points.text: 0° - 90°: All ratios positive

points.label: Quadrant II
points.text: 90° - 180°: Only sin and cosec positive

points.label: Quadrant III
points.text: 180° - 270°: Only tan and cot positive

points.label: Quadrant IV
points.text: 270° - 360°: Only cos and sec positive

example.problem: From Kavya's position, the elevation angle to the peak is 30°. Horizontal distance to peak base = 1000 m. Find peak height h.
In a right triangle, opposite = 8, hypotenuse = 17. Find sin θ, cos θ, tan θ, and θ itself.
From a cliff 100 meters high, Kavya sees a boat at an angle of depression 30°. How far is the boat from the cliff's base?

points.text: sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj
Standard values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° are essential
sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 (fundamental identity)
sin θ = cos(90° - θ) (complementary angles)
Applications: heights, distances, elevation/depression angles

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Construction Site
hook: A construction supervisor uses trigonometry to verify building heights and distances.

slides.title: Applications of Trigonometry: Heights and Distances
Building Height Verification
slides.storyContext: Arjun is supervising construction of a 50-story building in Mumbai. The architect claims the building is 200 meters tall. Arjun stands 100 meters away and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 63.4°. He uses trigonometry to verify the architect's claim!

slides.title: Angle of Elevation

points.label: Definition
points.text: The angle above the horizontal when looking up at an object.

points.label: Setup
points.text: Observer at ground level, looking up at a building or mountain peak.

points.label: Formula
points.text: tan(angle) = height/horizontal distance

slides.inSimpleWords: The angle your eyes tilt up when looking at something tall.

points.label: Definition
points.text: The angle below the horizontal when looking down at an object.

points.label: Key Property
points.text: Angle of depression from A to B = Angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

points.label: Formula
points.text: tan(angle) = height/horizontal distance (same as elevation)

example.problem: From a bridge 80m above water, the angle of depression to a boat is 20°. How far is the boat from the bridge (horizontally)?

slides.title: Solving Heights and Distances: Single Observation Point

points.label: Given
points.text: Distance from object, angle of elevation/depression

points.label: Find
points.text: Height or horizontal distance

points.label: Method
points.text: Use tan θ = opp/adj, solve for unknown

slides.inSimpleWords: One angle and one distance tells you the missing dimension.

example.problem: Arjun stands 100m from building, angle of elevation = 63.4°. Verify height is 200m. Find actual height: h = 100 × tan(63.4°).
example.solution: tan(63.4°) ≈ 2.0 → h = 100 × 2.0 = 200 meters. ✓ Architect's claim is correct!

slides.title: Two Observation Points Problem

points.label: Setup
points.text: Two observers at different positions measure angles to the same object.

points.label: Example
points.text: Two towers measure angles to a distant mountain peak from 500m apart.

points.label: Method
points.text: Set up two equations with unknown height, solve simultaneously using trigonometry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiple angles from different spots give you enough info to find an object's height.

example.problem: A flagpole is observed from two points A and B on the same side, 50m apart. From A, angle of elevation is 45°. From B (closer), angle is 60°. Find flagpole height.

points.label: Bearing
points.text: Direction measured clockwise from North (0° to 360°)

points.label: Example
points.text: East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°

points.label: Use in navigation
points.text: Combined with distances to locate positions

example.problem: A ship sails from port A toward east for 120 km, then turns north and sails 160 km to reach port B. A distant lighthouse L has bearing 30° from B and bearing 120° from A. Use trigonometry to find distances to L.
example.solution: This is a 2-point trigonometric problem. Requires setting up coordinate system with A at origin, east as +x, north as +y. Calculate using angle bisectors and sine rule in the triangle formed.

points.text: Angle of elevation: angle looking UP from horizontal
Angle of depression: angle looking DOWN from horizontal
tan θ = height/horizontal distance (fundamental formula)
Two-point problems: use two equations with common unknown
Applications: surveying, navigation, construction, astronomy

subject: Mathematics
title: Zara's Clock Shop
hook: A shopkeeper uses circle properties to design and repair clock faces.

slides.title: Designing a New Clock Face
slides.storyContext: Zara is designing a clock face where hour markers are evenly spaced on a circle of radius 10 cm. There are 12 hour markers, so each is 30° apart (360°/12 = 30°). She needs to find the arc length between markers and the chord distance.

slides.title: Circle Definition and Basic Elements

points.label: Circle
points.text: Locus of all points at a fixed distance (radius r) from a center O.

points.label: Diameter
points.text: Longest chord, passing through center. d = 2r

points.label: Arc
points.text: Portion of circle's circumference

points.label: Chord
points.text: Line segment joining any two points on circle

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle is all points equally far from a center point.

slides.title: Circumference and Arc Length

points.label: Circumference
points.text: C = 2πr or C = πd

points.label: Arc length
points.text: l = (θ/360°) × 2πr, where θ is central angle in degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: Arc length is proportional to the angle it subtends at center.

points.label: Equal chords
points.text: Chords of equal length subtend equal angles at center

points.label: Perpendicular from center
points.text: Perpendicular from center bisects the chord

points.label: Example
points.text: Clock markers at 30° apart create equal chords in the circle

example.problem: In circle with r=5cm, find chord length for central angle 60°
example.solution: Using chord formula: chord = 2r sin(θ/2) = 2(5) sin(30°) = 10(1/2) = 5 cm

slides.title: Sector and Segment Area

points.label: Sector area
points.text: Area of 'pie slice' = (θ/360°) × πr²

points.label: Segment area
points.text: Area between chord and arc = Sector area - Triangle area

points.label: Clock example
points.text: Each hour section (30° sector) has area = (30/360) × π(10)² = 25π/3 ≈ 26.18 cm²

slides.inSimpleWords: Sector is like a pizza slice; segment is the curved part.

points.label: Central angle
points.text: Angle at center; subtends one arc

points.label: Inscribed angle
points.text: Angle at circumference; equals half the central angle subtending same arc

points.label: Angle in semicircle
points.text: Angle subtended by diameter at circumference is 90°

example.problem: Central angle = 60°. Find inscribed angle on same arc

points.label: Tangent
points.text: Line touching circle at exactly one point, perpendicular to radius at that point

points.label: Two tangents
points.text: From external point, two tangents have equal length

points.label: Example
points.text: Clock handle at edge is tangent to the circle

example.problem: Zara's clock: r=10cm, 12 hour markers. (1) Circumference? (2) Arc between adjacent markers? (3) Chord length between adjacent markers? (4) Area of each sector?
Two circles of radius 5cm each have centers 6cm apart. Find the length of their common chord.
example.solution: Using Pythagorean theorem: If d=6, r=5, then half-chord length h: 5² = 3² + h² → h² = 16 → h = 4. Common chord = 8cm.

points.text: Circle: all points equidistant from center
Arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr
Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²
Chord = 2r sin(θ/2), where θ is central angle
Inscribed angle = half the central angle (same arc)

subject: Mathematics
title: Deepak's Garden Makeover
hook: A gardener calculates areas of circular flower beds and surrounding paths.

slides.title: Areas Related to Circles: Sectors and Segments
Circular Garden Design
slides.storyContext: Deepak is designing a circular flower garden with radius 5 meters in Deepak's backyard. He wants to calculate: (1) total area of the garden, (2) area of a quarter-circle flower section, (3) area of a pathway around it. His daughter asks: how much soil do we need for the flowers?

slides.title: Area of Circle

points.label: Formula
points.text: A = πr² (where r is radius)

points.label: Using diameter
points.text: A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4

points.label: Example
points.text: Garden with r=5m: A = π(25) = 25π ≈ 78.54 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Circle area equals π times radius squared.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Sector is a 'pie slice' of the circle from center

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr², where θ is central angle in degrees

points.label: Example
points.text: Quarter-circle (90°) in garden: A = (90/360) × 25π = 25π/4 ≈ 19.63 m²

example.problem: Sector with r=6cm and central angle 120°. Find area.

slides.title: Area of Segment

points.label: Definition
points.text: Segment is region between chord and arc (curved part without the triangle)

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area of segment = Area of sector - Area of triangle

points.label: Example
points.text: If sector angle = 60°: Area of triangle = (1/2)r²sin(60°) = (1/2)(25)(√3/2) = 25√3/4. Segment = (60/360)×25π - 25√3/4

slides.inSimpleWords: Segment area = pie slice area minus the triangle inside it.

example.problem: Circle r=7cm, chord at central angle 90°. Find segment area.
example.solution: Sector area = (90/360) × π(49) = 49π/4. Triangle (right angle at center) area = (1/2)(7)(7) = 49/2. Segment area = 49π/4 - 49/2 = 49(π/4 - 1/2) ≈ 9.76 cm²

slides.title: Area of Ring (Annulus)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Area between two concentric circles

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area = π(R² - r²), where R is outer radius, r is inner radius

points.label: Example
points.text: Pathway around garden: outer radius 6m, inner 5m. Area = π(36 - 25) = 11π ≈ 34.56 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Ring area = big circle minus small circle inside.

points.label: Combined areas
points.text: Find areas of overlapping/combined circular regions

points.label: Example
points.text: Semicircle + rectangle, or sector + triangle patterns

example.problem: Garden design: Circle r=5m (flowers), surrounding pathway (ring) with outer r=6m (grass), and one quarter-sector (90°) for vegetables. Calculate: (1) Flower area, (2) Grass pathway area, (3) Vegetable sector area, (4) Total area. Cost: ₹100/m² for flowers, ₹50/m² for grass, ₹75/m² for vegetables.
Two equal circles r=4cm intersect. Distance between centers = 4cm. Find total area of union (covered region).
example.solution: Each circle contributes a segment. Using chord at distance 2 from center: segment angle = 120° per circle. Area = 2 × [Sector(120°) - Triangle] = 2 × [16π/3 - 4√3] = 32π/3 - 8√3 ≈ 20.15cm²

points.text: Area of circle: A = πr²
Area of sector: (θ/360°) × πr²
Area of segment = Sector area - Triangle area
Area of ring/annulus: π(R² - r²)
Always break complex shapes into simpler geometric pieces

subject: Mathematics
title: Nisha's Packaging Business
hook: An entrepreneur calculates surface areas and volumes for shipping containers.

slides.title: Surface Areas and Volumes of 3D Shapes
Designing Shipping Containers
slides.storyContext: Nisha runs a packaging business in Delhi. She receives an order for 1000 cylindrical containers (radius 5cm, height 20cm) for a beverage company. She needs to calculate: (1) Volume of liquid each holds, (2) Surface area to know how much plastic is needed. She starts with a formula chart.

slides.title: Volume and Surface Area: Cuboid (Box)

points.label: Volume
points.text: V = l × b × h (length × breadth × height)

points.label: Surface Area
points.text: SA = 2(lb + bh + hl)

slides.inSimpleWords: Volume is space inside; surface area is total material needed.

points.label: Volume
points.text: V = πr²h

points.label: Curved Surface Area
points.text: CSA = 2πrh

points.label: Total Surface Area
points.text: TSA = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r)

points.label: Example
points.text: Cylinder r=5cm, h=20cm: V = π(25)(20) = 500π cm³, TSA = 2π(5)(20+5) = 250π cm²

example.problem: Find TSA of cylinder r=3cm, h=10cm

points.label: Volume
points.text: V = (1/3)πr²h

points.label: Slant height
points.text: l = √(r² + h²)

points.label: Curved Surface Area
points.text: CSA = πrl

points.label: Total Surface Area
points.text: TSA = πrl + πr²

example.problem: Cone r=4cm, h=3cm. Find slant height and CSA

points.label: Volume
points.text: V = (4/3)πr³

points.label: Surface Area
points.text: SA = 4πr²

example.problem: Sphere r=3cm. Find volume and SA

slides.title: Composite Solids

points.label: Combination
points.text: Shapes made of two or more basic solids joined together

points.label: Method
points.text: Calculate volume/area of each part, then add or subtract appropriately

points.label: Example
points.text: Cylinder with hemisphere on top (capsule shape)

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex shapes = sum/difference of simpler shapes.

example.problem: Cylindrical container r=5cm, h=20cm. Cost of plastic: ₹0.50 per cm². She needs 1000 containers. (1) Volume per container? (2) TSA per container? (3) Total plastic needed? (4) Total cost?
A toy is made of hemisphere (r=3cm) joined to cone (r=3cm, h=4cm). Find total surface area.
example.solution: Hemisphere CSA = 2π(9) = 18π. Cone slant height l = √(9+16) = 5. Cone CSA = π(3)(5) = 15π. Total = 18π + 15π = 33π ≈ 103.67 cm²

example.problem: A cylinder has radius 4cm and height 8cm. If radius is doubled but height is halved, how does volume change?
example.solution: Original V = π(16)(8) = 128π. New V = π(64)(4) = 256π. Change = 256π/128π = 2 times (volume doubles).

points.text: Cuboid: V = lbh, SA = 2(lb+bh+hl)
Cylinder: V = πr²h, TSA = 2πr(h+r)
Cone: V = (1/3)πr²h, TSA = πr(l+r), where l = √(r²+h²)
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, SA = 4πr²
Composite solids: break into parts, calculate, combine

subject: Mathematics
title: Rahul's School Survey
hook: A student uses statistics to analyze test scores and class performance data.

slides.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode, and Distribution
Analyzing Class Test Scores
slides.storyContext: Rahul is analyzing his class's mathematics test scores. The marks of 20 students are: 45, 52, 68, 75, 80, 62, 58, 72, 88, 65, 90, 78, 55, 69, 84, 76, 95, 60, 71, 82. Rahul wants to find: What's the average score? Who's in the middle? Is there a most common score range?

slides.title: Mean (Average)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Sum of all values divided by number of values

points.label: Formula
points.text: Mean = (Σx) / n

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is the average of all values.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Middle value when data is arranged in order

points.label: For even n
points.text: Average of two middle values

points.label: For odd n
points.text: The middle value

points.label: Example
points.text: 20 students (even): arrange scores in order, find average of 10th and 11th values

example.problem: Find median of: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30

slides.title: Mode

points.label: Definition
points.text: Value that appears most frequently

points.label: No mode
points.text: If all values appear with same frequency

points.label: Bimodal/Multimodal
points.text: If multiple values have highest frequency

points.label: Example
points.text: If 75 appears 3 times and all others once, mode = 75

slides.inSimpleWords: Mode is the most common value in the data.

points.label: Range
points.text: Difference between maximum and minimum: Range = Max - Min

points.label: Example
points.text: Test scores: Max=95, Min=45. Range = 50

points.label: Quartiles
points.text: Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (median), Q3 (75th percentile)

points.label: IQR
points.text: Interquartile range = Q3 - Q1

slides.title: Grouped Data: Class Intervals

points.label: Class
points.text: Range of values: e.g., 40-50, 50-60, 60-70

points.label: Class mark
points.text: (Lower limit + Upper limit)/2

points.label: Frequency
points.text: Number of values in each class

points.label: Example
points.text: 60-70 class has 5 students (frequency = 5)

slides.inSimpleWords: Group data into ranges to see distribution patterns.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Mean = (Σ(class mark × frequency)) / (Σ frequency)

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Find class mark for each class

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Multiply class mark by frequency

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Sum all products and divide by total frequency

example.problem: Class 0-10 (freq 5), 10-20 (freq 8), 20-30 (freq 7). Find mean.
Class test grouped: 40-50 (3 students), 50-60 (4), 60-70 (5), 70-80 (5), 80-90 (2), 90-100 (1). Find mean, median class, modal class.
Two classes took same test. Class A: mean = 75, range = 30. Class B: mean = 72, range = 50. Which class performed more consistently?
example.solution: Class A has smaller range (30 < 50), so scores are less spread out. Class A is more consistent even though mean is slightly higher.

points.text: Mean: sum of all values / number of values
Median: middle value when arranged in order
Mode: most frequently occurring value
Range: max - min (spread of data)
Grouped data uses class marks and frequencies for calculations

subject: Mathematics
title: Aditya's Cricket Tournament
hook: A cricket fan uses probability to predict match outcomes and tournament chances.

slides.title: Predicting Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Aditya is analyzing a cricket tournament with 4 teams: India, Australia, England, Pakistan. Each team has equal chance of winning. Aditya's school team, India, is playing. What's the probability India wins? What if there's an elimination tournament with 2 matches?

slides.title: Probability Definition

points.label: Probability
points.text: P(E) = (Number of favorable outcomes) / (Total number of possible outcomes)

points.label: Certain event
points.text: P = 1 (always happens)

points.label: Impossible event
points.text: P = 0 (never happens)

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the chance that something will happen.

slides.title: Sample Space and Events

points.label: Sample space
points.text: All possible outcomes: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} for a die

points.label: Event
points.text: Subset of sample space: E = {even numbers} = {2, 4, 6}

points.label: Cricket example
points.text: Tournament: S = {India wins, Australia wins, England wins, Pakistan wins}

slides.inSimpleWords: Sample space is all possibilities; event is what we're interested in.

points.label: Theoretical
points.text: Based on logical reasoning: P(H) = 1/2 for fair coin

points.label: Experimental
points.text: Based on actual trials: flip 100 times, count heads

points.label: Law of Large Numbers
points.text: Experimental probability approaches theoretical with more trials

example.problem: Fair die: P(rolling 3)? vs. Roll die 60 times, count 3s?
example.solution: Theoretical: P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Experimental: If we get 12 threes, P ≈ 12/60 = 1/5 = 0.20 (close to theoretical).

slides.title: Compound Events: AND (Intersection)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Both events happen: P(A and B)

points.label: Independent events
points.text: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

points.label: Example
points.text: Toss coin AND roll die: P(H and 3) = P(H) × P(3) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability of both things happening = multiply individual probabilities.

points.label: Definition
points.text: At least one event happens: P(A or B)

points.label: Formula
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) [if not mutually exclusive]

points.label: Mutually exclusive
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) [if A and B can't both happen]

points.label: Example
points.text: Die: P(odd or prime) = P(odd) + P(prime) - P(odd AND prime) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3

example.problem: 4 teams, equal chance. (1) P(India wins first match)? (2) P(India wins 2 consecutive matches)? (3) P(India doesn't win)?
Standard 52-card deck. (1) P(drawing a king)? (2) P(drawing red card or ace)?
example.solution: (1) 4 kings in deck: P = 4/52 = 1/13 ≈ 0.077. (2) Red cards = 26, Aces (extra black) = 2. P(red) = 26/52, P(black ace) = 2/52. P(red or ace) = 26/52 + 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13 ≈ 0.538

example.problem: Bag: 5 red, 3 blue balls. Draw 2 balls. P(both red) WITH replacement? WITHOUT replacement?
example.solution: WITH replacement: P = 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64 ≈ 0.391. WITHOUT replacement: P = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14 ≈ 0.357 (slightly lower, as fewer red balls remain).

points.text: Probability: P(E) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Complement: P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
